title: What an IES File Stores
abstract: A careful reading of LM-63 photometric data: metadata, lamp and multiplier fields, vertical and horizontal angles, candela tables, symmetry, and the distinction between a measured distribution and an engine texture.
imageAlt: An IES photometric file is parsed into angle arrays and a candela intensity table
lede: An IES file is not a picture of a light beam and not a PSF. In the common LM-63 family, it is an electronic description of measured photometric intensity around a luminaire, plus metadata and test configuration. A renderer turns those irregular angular samples into a representation convenient for its own light shader.

sections.heading: The physical quantity is luminous intensity
paragraphs: The central table contains luminous intensity samples, normally interpreted in candelas after the file’s candela multiplier is applied. One candela is one lumen per steradian. The distribution answers: in this measured direction, how much luminous intensity does the luminaire emit?

It does not directly store illuminance on a wall, radiance along a camera ray, or a grayscale cookie image. Distance, orientation, fixture placement, and the renderer’s lighting model are applied later.

equations.label: Intensity sample after file scaling
equations.expression: I(theta, phi) = table(theta, phi) * candelaMultiplier * ballastFactor
terms: The exact use of lamp and ballast-related fields depends on the LM-63 revision and consuming application.
Do not silently multiply an engine light-intensity control a second time without defining the intended calibration.

sections.heading: The file is angles plus a rectangular table
paragraphs: After the header and luminaire/test fields, the file declares counts for vertical and horizontal angles. It then lists the vertical-angle array, the horizontal-angle array, and candela values for each horizontal plane across all vertical angles. The angular spacing may be non-uniform, so sample number is not itself an angle.

To evaluate an arbitrary direction, convert that direction into the file’s photometric coordinate system, find the surrounding vertical and horizontal samples, and interpolate. The photometric type field determines how the coordinate system is interpreted.

sections.heading: Symmetry is encoded by coverage
paragraphs: Many luminaires do not list a full 0–360-degree horizontal sweep. A restricted set of horizontal planes can imply rotational, bilateral, or quadrant symmetry under the standard’s conventions. A loader should reconstruct the intended domain before resampling, not clamp every missing direction to the nearest listed plane.

Vertical coverage also matters. Some measurements cover only the downward hemisphere; others include uplight. Validate monotonic angles, declared counts, table length, and expected coverage before generating a texture.

callouts.title: Parser rule
callouts.text: Do not assume 1-degree samples, a 256×256 grid, or a full sphere. Those are possible runtime representations, not properties guaranteed by LM-63 data.

sections.heading: File data and Unreal’s runtime representation are different
paragraphs: Unreal imports an IES profile and builds a texture used by the light. Epic’s documentation describes its representation as a one-dimensional texture swept around an axis. That is an engine choice suited to the supported profile behavior; it is not a claim that the source file contains one-dimensional pixels.

A custom implementation may instead resample intensity into a 2D angular texture—for example, u from vertical angle and v from azimuth. That can preserve asymmetric distributions, but it must define axis orientation, seam wrapping, pole behavior, interpolation, normalization, and the relationship between stored candelas and the light component’s own intensity controls.

sections.heading: A small validation suite
paragraphs: Test a rotationally symmetric profile, an asymmetric profile, a profile with incomplete horizontal coverage, and a file with a non-trivial candela multiplier. Compare original tabulated directions exactly before judging interpolated directions. Plot polar slices at several horizontal planes so swapped axes and mirrored azimuth become obvious.

Keep raw parsed values alongside the generated texture in debug builds. When the rendered beam looks wrong, this lets the investigation distinguish parser error, coordinate error, resampling error, and lighting-model error.
bullets: Declared angle counts equal parsed angle counts.
Angles are monotonic and within the expected photometric domain.
Texture samples at listed directions reproduce scaled source values within tolerance.
Integrated or peak intensity behavior is documented when normalization is applied.

sections.heading: Parser acceptance criteria
paragraphs: A parser fixture passes when it identifies the LM-63 revision, consumes the declared number of angles and candela samples, preserves raw values, reconstructs the intended horizontal coverage, and reproduces every tabulated direction after documented multipliers. Texture generation is a later test layer.
bullets: Reject truncated tables and non-monotonic angle arrays.
Keep photometric type and TILT handling visible in debug output.
Plot source planes before interpolating between them.
Store the import transformation with the generated asset.

closing: Parser output should remain an angle-indexed candela table. The engine-specific 1D or 2D texture is a documented resampling product, not the source format.
